newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African National Party "shocked" by Tutu attack.
newsitem.headline: S.African National Party "shocked" by Tutu attack.

text.p: South Africa's opposition National Party said on Friday it was temporarily boycotting the truth commission because of an emotional attack on it by the body's chairman Archbishop Desmond Tutu.

"We are suspending contact for the moment," said party (NP) spokesman Jan Bosman, elaborating on a statement which said the party was "distancing itself" from the commission until Tutu retracted his attack.

"The shocking statement by Archbishop Tutu and Deputy Chairman of the Truth and Reconciliation Commission Alex Boraine indicating that they have already found the NP and F.W. de Klerk guilty of all atrocities committed during the apartheid era is a travesty of what was intended by the commission process," the statement said.
Tutu told a news conference on Thursday that testimony to the commission on Wednesday by de Klerk, leader of the NP and the last white president, was unacceptable.

Tutu said he had nearly broken down in tears when de Klerk maintained that torture and murder were never government policy during the apartheid years. Boraine made similar comments, dismissing de Klerk's testimony as a waste of time.
The NP statement said Tutu and Boraine had pre-empted the final report of the commission, which is due out next year.

"They have...rejected de Klerk's earnest apology. They have thrown his acknowledgement of political and moral responsibility back in his face and they are misrepresenting what he actually said," the party said.
It said Tutu and Boraine had ignored legislation which set up their commission and requires them to be impartial and to make findings only after hearing all the evidence.

"(They) are clearly showing their prejudice by making these premature statements...The National Party believes it has no option but to apply to court to force the commission to comply with the Act (which set up the commission)," the statement said.

The opposition Democratic Party, heirs to the notable anti-apartheid campaigner Helen Suzman, said the truth commission had played into the hands of the NP's strategy of "obscuring its own accountability".

"However regrettable we or the commission may find this, the final and full picture can only emerge at the end of the commission process and Archbishop Tutu's response, however understandable, was premature," a statement said.
"De Klerk is fully within his rights in putting the picture to the commission as he interprets it... He clearly doesn't intend to compromise any future defence he may have to mount in court."

Independent political analysts said the NP, no matter what its human rights record, had a point in accusing the commission of bias. They said there was little chance that any form of reconciliation would flow from its activities.

The commission was set up by President Nelson Mandela in 1995 to uncover as much as possible of the crimes and human rights violations committed by all sides during apartheid, in the hope that revealing the truth would heal the wounds from that era.
